buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus (archaic)
buildings.summary: The great Etruscan-plan temple of the Capitoline Triad, vowed by Tarquinius Priscus, built by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus on 13 September 509 BC. The largest temple of its age in Italy: a cappellaccio podium about 53 x 62 m carrying a deep porch of three rows of six widely spaced tufa columns, three cellae (Jupiter in the wider central one, flanked by Juno and Minerva) and a timber superstructure clad in painted terracottas by Vulca of Veii, crowned by a terracotta quadriga (bronze from 296 BC).

phases.t: dedicated by M. Horatius Pulvillus on the Ides of September
survives the Gallic sack while the Capitol holds out
the Ogulnii replace the terracotta quadriga with bronze
columns and walls whitened with stucco by the censors
burns on 6 July with the Sibylline Books

buildings.note: Centre and bearing derived from the excavated podium: the east flank exposed in the Esedra di Marco Aurelio (c. 12.48226, 41.89268) and the SE corner visible in Via del Tempio di Giove (c. 12.48253, 41.89223) give a flank bearing of c. 156; Platner-Ashby give the axis as 26.5 deg east of N-S, fronting south, i.e. a facade bearing of c. 154. Wikipedia's point (12.48167, 41.89222) lies c. 25 m WSW of this centre and probably marks the museum area. Podium 53.5 x 62.25 m (Mura Sommella); Etruscan plan with triple cella and three rows of six columns in the pronaos, colonnades down the flanks, blind rear wall.

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus (Sullan-Catulan)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt on the archaic foundations after the fire of 83 BC: Sulla began it, using marble column elements brought from the Olympieion at Athens, and Q. Lutatius Catulus dedicated it in 69 BC with gilded bronze roof tiles. Augustus restored it at great expense. It burned when the Vitellians stormed the Capitol in December 69.

phases.t: Sulla begins reconstruction
dedicated by Q. Lutatius Catulus
Augustan restoration (RG 20)
burned on 19 December in the fighting between Vitellians and Flavians

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus (Vespasianic)
buildings.summary: Vespasian cleared the ruins himself, carrying the first basket of rubble, and rebuilt the temple on the same plan but taller, the only change the haruspices allowed. It stood only a few years before the fire of 80 under Titus.

phases.t: lustration of the site on 21 June
destroyed in the three-day fire under Titus

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Domitian's rebuilding, said to have cost over 12,000 talents for the gilding alone, with fluted Pentelic marble columns about 2.1 m in diameter (a drum and an Attic base survive), gilded bronze roof tiles and gold-plated doors. Closed after 392; Stilicho stripped gold from the doors, Gaiseric carried off half the gilded tiles in 455, and it decayed into a quarry.

phases.t: dedicated by Domitian
pagan cult ends
Vandals remove half the gilded roof tiles
Narses reportedly removes statues

buildings.name: Area Capitolina (archaic precinct)
buildings.summary: The leveled summit precinct in front of the Capitoline temple, enclosed by a temenos wall whose foundation runs parallel to the temple rear.

phases.t: leveling and terracing of the Capitolium

buildings.note: Precinct drawn as a 100 x 112 m rectangle on the temple axis, from the rear temenos foundation to the brow of the Tarpeian cliff; the real outline followed the hilltop and is not known.

buildings.name: Area Capitolina (Republican precinct)
buildings.summary: After the Gallic sack the Capitol was walled with massive squared-stone substructures (Livy 6.4.12) and the area filled with temples, altars, statues and trophies.

phases.t: substructio saxo quadrato
Tiberius Gracchus killed by senators near the temple

buildings.name: Area Capitolina (imperial precinct)
buildings.summary: The Sullan-Catulan reconstruction re-laid the precinct; under the Empire it was crowded with dedications and dynastic statues. Abandoned after the 4th century.

phases.t: re-dedication with the temple
scene of the Vitellian assault

buildings.name: Hut of Romulus on the Capitol
buildings.summary: A thatched hut kept and renewed on the Capitol as a relic of Romulus, a twin of the better known Casa Romuli on the Palatine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 74
buildings.note: Exact site unknown; placed in the Area Capitolina SW of the temple.

buildings.name: Temple of Juno Moneta
buildings.summary: Vowed by L. Furius Camillus against the Aurunci in 345 BC and dedicated on 1 June 344 on the Arx, on the traditional site of the house of M. Manlius Capitolinus. The Roman mint was set up beside it in 269 BC, so that 'moneta' came to mean money.

phases.t: dedicated 1 June
silver coinage minted in the adjoining workshops
roof damaged by a storm

buildings.name: Mint at the Temple of Juno Moneta
buildings.summary: Workshops of the Republican mint beside the temple of Juno Moneta; the mint moved to the Caelian (Moneta Caesaris) under the Flavians.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 260

buildings.name: Auguraculum on the Arx
buildings.summary: The augurs' observation post on the northern summit of the Capitol, a consecrated open square from which they watched the birds over the Campus Martius and the Quirinal.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 46
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2014)

buildings.name: Asylum (grove between the two summits)
buildings.summary: The saddle between Arx and Capitolium, 'inter duos lucos', where Romulus was said to have opened an asylum for fugitives to people his city. A sacred grove covered it through the Republic.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 40
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2014)
buildings.note: Area of the modern Piazza del Campidoglio.

buildings.name: Asylum (grove after the Tabularium)
buildings.summary: After the Tabularium closed the saddle on the Forum side the grove survived as a smaller sacred area around the temple of Veiovis.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 40

buildings.name: Tabularium
buildings.summary: The great substructure building closing the Forum at the foot of the Capitol, built by Q. Lutatius Catulus in 78 BC after the fire of 83: a sheer peperino and tufa wall with small windows supporting an arcaded gallery framed by Doric half-columns, with a lost upper storey. Long identified as the state record office; it more likely carried a monumental passage between Arx and Capitolium.

phases.t: inscription of Catulus (CIL VI 1314)
later becomes the base of the Palazzo Senatorio

buildings.name: Temple of Veiovis (first)
buildings.summary: Vowed by L. Furius Purpurio at the battle of Cremona in 200/198 BC and dedicated in 192 'inter duos lucos', the god's second temple in Rome after the one on the Tiber island.

buildings.summary: Rebuilt with the Tabularium after 83 BC with a transverse cella about 15 x 9 m and a narrow tetrastyle porch, a plan forced by the cramped site; the cult statue of Veiovis was found in the cella.

buildings.name: Temple of Fides (first)
buildings.summary: Temple of Good Faith dedicated by A. Atilius Calatinus during the First Punic War next to the Capitoline temple; treaties and diplomatic bronzes were posted on its walls and the Senate sometimes met there.

buildings.name: Temple of Fides (Scaurus)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt by M. Aemilius Scaurus in 115 BC; architectural fragments found in the Area Capitolina have been attributed to it.

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Feretrius (archaic)
buildings.summary: The oldest shrine on the Capitol, said to have been founded by Romulus to house the spolia opima; Dionysius says its longer sides were under 15 feet.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 219
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Iuppiter Feretrius

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Feretrius (Augustan)
buildings.summary: Restored by Octavian at Atticus' suggestion when roofless and falling down; a denarius of 50 BC shows it as a tetrastyle shrine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 219

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Tonans
buildings.summary: Vowed by Augustus after lightning killed a slave in front of his litter in Cantabria and dedicated on 1 September 22 BC at the entrance to the Capitoline precinct; built of solid marble, it drew crowds away from Jupiter Optimus Maximus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 226
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Iuppiter Tonans

buildings.name: Temple of Venus Erycina (Capitol)
buildings.summary: Vowed by Q. Fabius Maximus after Trasimene and dedicated in 215 BC on the Capitol, beside the twin temple of Mens, separated from it by a water channel.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 408
buildings.note: Pair placed in the SW part of the Area Capitolina; positions conjectural.

buildings.name: Temple of Mens
buildings.summary: Temple of Right Thinking vowed by T. Otacilius Crassus after Trasimene and dedicated in 215 BC next to Venus Erycina; restored by M. Aemilius Scaurus in 107 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 250

buildings.name: Temple of Ops (Capitol)
buildings.summary: Temple of Ops Opifera near the Capitoline temple, where Caesar kept the state reserve; Antony seized 700 million sesterces from it after the Ides of March.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 277
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Ops

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Custos
buildings.summary: Domitian replaced the little shrine of Jupiter Conservator, built on the site of the house of the aedituus where he had hidden in December 69, with a large temple of Jupiter the Guardian showing himself in the god's lap.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 218
buildings.note: Site unknown; placed NW of the Capitoline temple.

buildings.name: Insula dell Aracoeli
buildings.summary: A Hadrianic apartment block at the foot of the Arx, preserved to its fifth storey against the cliff: shops on the street, mezzanines above and small flats on the upper floors. A rare surviving insula of the imperial city; the church of San Biagio de Mercato was later built into it.

phases.t: built (brick stamps)
church of San Biagio installed on the upper floors
